what_its_for: Goserelin is used to treat hormone-sensitive conditions. In men, it is used to treat prostate cancer by lowering the amount of testosterone in the body. In women, it is used to treat breast cancer, endometriosis (painful tissue growth outside the uterus), and uterine fibroids. It may also be used before certain uterine procedures. Goserelin works by signaling the body to reduce the production of sex hormones (testosterone in men and estrogen in women).
how_to_take: Goserelin comes as a small implant (pellet) that a doctor or nurse injects under the skin of your belly (abdomen). You do NOT inject this medicine yourself at home. Each injection is given in a medical office or clinic. The injection may cause mild discomfort, bruising, or swelling at the site. Do not rub the area after the injection. If you notice unusual pain, redness, or swelling at the injection site, contact your doctor.
dosing: The most common doses are 3.6 mg injected once every 28 days (about once a month), or 10.8 mg injected once every 3 months (about every 12 weeks). Your doctor will decide which dose and schedule is right for you based on your condition. It is very important to keep all of your scheduled injection appointments so the medicine works properly.
missed_dose: Because goserelin is given by a healthcare provider in a clinic or office, missing a dose means missing your scheduled appointment. Try not to miss or delay any appointments. If you have to reschedule, call your doctor or clinic as soon as possible to arrange a new time. Missing doses can reduce how well the medicine works and may allow hormone levels to rise again.
storage: Goserelin implants are stored at room temperature (below 77°F or 25°C) and are kept by the pharmacy or medical office — you do not need to store this medicine at home. Keep the implant away from heat, light, and moisture until it is used. Do not freeze it.
what_to_avoid: Tell your doctor about all medicines, vitamins, and supplements you take before starting goserelin. Avoid becoming pregnant while using this medicine — goserelin can harm an unborn baby. Women who could become pregnant should use non-hormonal birth control (such as condoms or a diaphragm) during treatment and for a short time after stopping. Do not use hormonal birth control (pills, patches, rings) without asking your doctor first. Avoid smoking, as it can increase certain risks while on this type of therapy.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away if you experience: sudden weakness or numbness in your arms or legs; difficulty walking or moving; chest pain, shortness of breath, or signs of a blood clot; severe bone pain; signs of high blood sugar such as increased thirst, frequent urination, or blurred vision; mood changes, depression, or thoughts of self-harm; signs of a heart problem such as irregular heartbeat or swelling in your legs; vaginal bleeding that is unexpected or heavy; signs of an allergic reaction such as rash, hives, swelling of the face or throat, or difficulty breathing; or pain, bleeding, or a lump at the injection site that does not go away.
when_it_works: Goserelin begins working within a few days by changing your hormone levels. However, you may not feel better right away. In men with prostate cancer, testosterone levels usually drop to very low levels within 2 to 4 weeks. In women, estrogen levels typically fall to menopausal levels within 3 to 4 weeks. Symptoms from your condition may take several weeks or months to improve. For some conditions like endometriosis, pain relief may be noticed within the first 1 to 2 months of treatment. Talk to your doctor if you have concerns about how the medicine is working for you.
special_populations: Older adults: Goserelin is commonly used in older men with prostate cancer and is generally safe, but older adults should be monitored for bone thinning (osteoporosis), heart health, and blood sugar changes. Women: Goserelin causes a temporary menopause-like state. This can cause hot flashes, mood swings, vaginal dryness, and bone loss. Long-term use (more than 6 months) for endometriosis is generally not recommended without careful evaluation because of the risk of bone thinning. Talk to your doctor about calcium and vitamin D supplements to protect your bones. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Do NOT use goserelin if you are pregnant, as it may harm the baby. If you think you are pregnant, contact your doctor immediately. It is not known if goserelin passes into breast milk, so breastfeeding is not recommended during treatment. Children: Goserelin is not typically used in children except in very specific situations under specialist care.
